paragraphs.heading: Salt from the sea
paragraphs.text: Sea salt is salt made by evaporating seawater. It also goes by the names bay salt and solar salt. People use it to season food, in cooking and cosmetics, and to preserve food. Its production has been dated to prehistoric times, as has that of mined rock salt.

paragraphs.heading: What is in it
paragraphs.text: The main component of sea salt is sodium chloride. Other salts make up the rest, anywhere from under 0.2 to 22%. Most of these are chloride and sulfate salts of calcium, potassium and magnesium. There are also much smaller amounts of many of the trace elements that natural seawater contains. Sea salts sold today vary widely in their chemical composition, even though natural saltwater has a relatively constant ionic composition.

paragraphs.heading: Sun or fuel
paragraphs.text: The principle of making sea salt is to evaporate the water out of sea brine. In warm, dry climates solar energy alone may do the whole job. In other climates fuel has been used. Modern sea salt production is found almost entirely in Mediterranean and other warm, dry climates.

paragraphs.heading: A saltworks on The Wash
paragraphs.text: Around The Wash in eastern England, salt was made this way in the Roman and medieval periods. The tide brought the brine, and the fens and moors supplied peat for fuel. The sun did most of the evaporating of the dilute sea brine. Workers scraped up the concentrated slurry of salt and mud and washed it with clean sea water, so that impurities settled out. They poured the brine into shallow pans of lightly baked local clay, which stood over a peat fire, on clay pillars the size of a fist, for the final evaporation. The dried salt was then scraped out and sold.

paragraphs.heading: Salt from ashes
paragraphs.text: The Visayas Islands of the Philippines have a different tradition. Coconut husks, driftwood or other plant matter are left to soak in seawater for several months at least and then burned to ash. More seawater is filtered through the ashes, and the brine that results is evaporated in containers. The practice is endangered because of competition from cheap, industrially produced salt. Only two traditions survive today: asín tibuok and túltul.

paragraphs.heading: Sea salt and table salt
paragraphs.text: Sea salt and table salt have about the same nutritional value, since both are primarily sodium chloride. Table salt is more processed, to remove minerals, and usually has something added to stop it clumping, such as silicon dioxide. Human health depends on the element iodine, and sea salt holds only small amounts of it. Iodised salt is table salt with a minute amount of iodine salts mixed in. On taste and texture, some gourmets believe sea salt is the better of the two.

paragraphs.heading: What the label does not say
paragraphs.text: In the US, salt labelled “sea salt” might not actually be from the sea. It only has to meet the FDA’s purity requirements. In another sense, though, every mined salt was once a sea salt. At some point in the distant past, mined salts originated in a marine source, usually a shallow sea that was evaporating.
